title: Long-Term Fleet Maintenance of Hydroelectric Generators Using Proportional Hazard Model and Nonlinear Programming
contribution: Builds a statistics-to-NLP pipeline (Kaplan-Meier, Cox PHM with load covariate, renewal-reward cost rates) to plan overhauls of 90 hydro generator units over 50 years, solved by relaying Lindo API (SLP/GRG) for feasibility and NOMAD for polishing, and shows that +50% load moves withdrawals about 10 years earlier.
problem_entry: Application-driven: aging fleets reach end of life together, so plant-level resource limits make the standard age-replacement policy infeasible; a mathematical-programming framework is proposed (p. 7).
key_idea: Separable fleet cost-rate objective with one replacement period per unit (n=90) under crew/crane/capacity/budget constraints; Lindo finds a feasible plan and NOMAD restarted from it lowers J (7.709->7.566 k$/h) (pp. 14-17).
assumptions: All components of a unit replaced together, load the only covariate with constant base hazard 'for the sake of simplicity', Gompertz-Makeham law, approximate costs; EB/PB choice for NOMAD not stated (pp. 7, 11, 16).
proof_devices: renewal-reward cost rate C(tau)/l(tau) and the classical optimal-age condition from Barlow et al. (eqs. 8-11, p. 12)
experiments: One run per setting on a workstation: NOMAD from the infeasible 50-year plan finds no feasible point (10^4 evals, then a larger run whose count lost its exponent in extraction); Lindo status 5 feasible; NOMAD from Lindo's plan improves by 143 $/h with 50,000 evals in 33 min; no seeds or profiles (pp. 16-19).
positioning: Short review of generator maintenance scheduling (0-1 IP, DP, Benders, stochastic programming) without critique; NOMAD/MADS and Lindo presented as two tools (pp. 8, 15).
writing: Engineering application report; claims about solver behaviour descriptive only; internal inconsistencies (3 problems announced, 2 reported; '+50%' later called 'doubling'; Lindo time 17 min vs 6.17) (pp. 16-19).
limits_future: 'limited only by the ability of nonlinear solvers'; future: whole fleet (300+ units), more general policies and cost structures; NOMAD's feasibility failure not analysed (pp. 16-20).

method_links.note: Quantifiable constraints, infeasible x0, no stated EB/PB choice and no PB or LH-search remedy tried when NOMAD stalls, contrary to the group's manual (S202 p. 74).
n=90 exceeds the ~20 variables where the manual calls NOMAD efficient; SLP/GRG reached feasibility where NOMAD did not in Problem I (inference, not drawn by the paper).
Evaluation counts and wall-clock reported but single runs, no profiles, solvers chained rather than compared.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Lindo (SLP/GRG) supplies a feasible plan, NOMAD restarted from it polishes; done for both Problems I and II

transferable: If direct search cannot reach feasibility from an infeasible start, hand it a feasible point from another solver and report the direct-search gain with its evaluation cost separately (pp. 17-19).
Report decision-level indicators (reliability at withdrawal AURI, of the remaining fleet AFRI) next to the objective to distinguish near-equal-cost plans (pp. 16-19).

quotes.text: This is an ideal context to the so-called direct search algorithms which uses only functions evaluations to find the best solution.
This gain is however obtained at the cost of 50000 function evaluations in 33 minutes (Figure 9).

title: Optimization of algorithms with OPAL
contribution: Presents OPAL, a Python modelling layer that turns algorithm-parameter tuning into a constrained blackbox problem solved by NOMAD/MADS, with typed parameters (incl. categorical), composite performance measures, static surrogates, parallelism and a clustering-based representative-subset surrogate (read as GERAD G-2012-08).
problem_entry: Autotuning frameworks use heuristics, coordinate search, Nelder-Mead or random search; OPAL enters by using a method with strong convergence theory, non-intrusively (p. 8).
key_idea: Formulate tuning as min psi(p) s.t. p in P, phi(p) in M over atomic/composite measures, gate p in P before launching the target, separate model structure from model data, and feed static surrogates to NOMAD (pp. 9-10, 13-15).
assumptions: Real/integer/binary/categorical parameters; target may fail or stall; CPU-time objective is not even a function; no convergence hypotheses beyond the summarized MADS ladder (pp. 9-11).
proof_devices: none new; summary of the MADS hierarchy (Clarke on hypertangent directions if Lipschitz, gradient zero / contingent KKT if strictly differentiable, no stagnation at strict maximizers or saddles) (p. 11)
experiments: No systematic benchmark or rival tuner; IPOPT case (6 params, 730 CUTEr problems): 207,866 -> 198,615 evaluations in 27h55m with 10 concurrent evals; SOM surrogate with 41 problems in 4h17m lands 'close to' it (p. 17).
positioning: Positions against heuristic autotuners (ATLAS, PHiPAC, OSKI etc.) by method quality and against its own 2006/2010/2011 predecessors by features (p. 8).
writing: Tool paper with code listings for a toy (finite-difference step) and for a CUTEr trust-region tuning; convergence theory used as a selling argument; listing slips (phi>=0 vs (None,get_error,0); undefined 'problems') (pp. 13-16).
limits_future: Future: robust parameter values and automatic identification of the most influential parameters; no stated limitation of results (p. 18).

method_links.note: Algorithm tuned as a blackbox by MADS; lineage 2006 -> 2010 -> 2011 -> 2012.
Domain checked before launch, failures modelled, EB/PB/filter/hidden distinguished, no-failure requirement as an explicit constraint.
Surrogates only seed a side problem or order/generate candidates inside the solver.
OPAL's value rests on NOMAD features (variable types, groups, periodic variables, surrogates, constraint types).
Convergence ladder used as an argument against heuristic tuners, with no proof and no controlled comparison.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Representativeness over size for test sets
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: SOM clustering reduces 730 CUTEr problems to 41 representatives used as a static surrogate (27h55m vs 4h17m)
p in P verified without launching the target algorithm; infeasible p discarded at no cost

transferable: When the blackbox is 'run an algorithm over a test set', cluster the test set and keep one representative per cluster as a static surrogate; report full vs surrogate wall-clock and closeness (p. 17).
Encode 'the tuned algorithm must still solve every problem' as a constraint (#failures <= 0), not a penalty in the objective (pp. 15-17).
Separate problem structure (objective/constraint form) from data (target, instance list) so variants need one-line changes (p. 14).

quotes.text: By contrast, Opal uses a solid optimization method supported by a strong convergence theory, yielding solutions that are local minimizers in a meaningful sense.
It is important to stress that our framework does not assume correctness of the target algorithm, or even that it execute at all.

title: Ordering 15 marbles with a three-way scale
contribution: Shows that 15 distinct marbles can always be sorted with at most 20 weighings of a three-tray ranking scale, against a counting lower bound of 16, leaving the gap open (read as GERAD G-2013-05).
problem_entry: A twist on classical balance puzzles: the scale ranks three marbles; minimize worst-case weighings for 15 (pp. 5-6).
key_idea: Chains and v-chains plus Lemma 2.2 (two chains + a v-chain of p marbles in p-2 weighings), pivot-partition strategies for small n, and a ladder of improving strategies 25 -> 23 -> 22 -> 20 (pp. 6-13).
assumptions: Distinct weights; each weighing returns the full order of three marbles; worst-case count (p. 6).
proof_devices: induction on the number of marbles for Lemma 2.2 (p. 6)
case analysis on the cardinality split around a pivot marble with symmetry WLOG (pp. 7-13)
information-theoretic counting bound ceil(log_6 p!) (Prop. 4.1, p. 14)
positioning: Self-contained; only a puzzle website is credited for the 7-marble strategy (p. 7).
writing: Short constructive proofs with small graphs; bound improvements presented as a sequence; honest open-question ending; label slips (Lemma 2.6/2.8 for Propositions) (pp. 7-14).
limits_future: Gap between 16 and 20 explicitly open; closing it would give the optimal strategy (p. 14). Later generalized by S177 (2025).

method_links.note: Claim bracketed by a constructive upper bound and a counting lower bound, gap stated rather than a smoothness ladder plus counterexamples.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Strategies giving 25, 23, 22 then 20 weighings, each unlocked by a new lemma

transferable: Write the counting bound ceil(log_k #outcomes) for your oracle before searching for strategies, then report the construction against it and state the gap (p. 14).
Present an upper bound as a ladder of improving strategies, each naming the lemma that buys the improvement (pp. 7-8, 13).

quotes.text: We do not know the answer to these questions.
Bridging the gap between these two bounds would give the optimal strategy.

title: NOMAD User Guide, Version 3.7.2
contribution: Duplicate Scholar entry of S019 (byte-identical text file, NOMAD 3.7.2 user guide); only cross-reading notes are added: XMesh from S061 is the 3.7.1 default, and OrthoMADS directions moved from Halton to a seeded PRNG.
problem_entry: Same as S019: defined by simulator pathologies and by when not to use NOMAD (p. 11).
key_idea: Same as S019; new here: ANISOTROPIC_MESH default yes (XMesh [26]) with the isotropic SMESH kept as a developer switch (pp. 80, 104, 110).
assumptions: Same as S019; new here: a single seed controls all random aspects and Halton directions are deprecated (p. 104).

method_links.note: S061's March 2014 preprint is the default mesh in the August 2015 guide.
OrthoMADS, introduced as deterministic, now draws directions from a seeded PRNG; repeatability rests on the seed, not on determinism.
Manual remedies (PB for difficult constraints, LH search without x0) serve as the yardstick against which S204 and S069 fall short.

transferable: When a paper changes a solver default, keep the old behaviour behind a named switch (USE_SMESH) so old results stay reproducible (p. 110).

quotes.text: OrthoMads directions are obtained by a pseudo-random number generator on a unit n-sphere. Halton directions are deprecated.
Use of a dynamic scaling of the mesh size per variable based on the direction of success during optimization (XMesh) [26].

title: Dynamic scaling in the mesh adaptive direct search algorithm for blackbox optimization
contribution: Replaces MADS's scalar mesh and poll sizes by per-variable vectors that are coarsened only along variables that moved on success, re-presents MADS from scratch, re-proves Clarke stationarity, and shows data-profile gains (about 10% more of 212 problems solved; better on a supersonic business jet MDO problem); became NOMAD's XMesh (read as GERAD G-2014-16).
problem_entry: Scaling strongly affects performance, default MADS keeps mesh aspect ratios fixed, and under a finite budget bad scaling makes progress marginal; also a wish to ease the MADS presentation (pp. 5-6).
key_idea: Mesh M^k = V^k + diag(delta^k) Z^n with delta_j = min(Delta0_j, Delta_j)^2/(sqrt(n) Delta0_j); on failure halve all Delta_j; on success increment r_j only if |d_j| > ||d||_inf/n, plus a catch-up rule; Householder directions stretched by diag(Delta) and rounded to the mesh (pp. 8-13).
assumptions: Extreme barrier only; feasible x0 with finite f; bounded iterates; beta_j^2 rational (defended as necessary via [4]); mechanism (5); dense refining directions, f Lipschitz near x*, nonempty hypertangent cone (pp. 7, 9-10, 18-20).
proof_devices: integer mesh-index representation Delta_j = Delta0_j beta_j^{r_j}, delta_j = delta0_j beta_j^{r_j-|r_j|} (Lemma 2.3, p. 9)
lattice-finiteness contradiction: bounded mesh index + rational beta^2 put all trial points on x0 + (delta0/q^rho)Z, boundedness leaves finitely many points (Prop. A.1, p. 19)
Clarke derivative lower bound along refining directions by choosing y=x^k, t=||v^k|| in the lim sup (Thm A.4, p. 20)
experiments: NOMAD 3.7.0 beta, OrthoMADS 2n, quadratic models disabled and a shared direction generator in both variants; 212 More-Wild instances x 10 seeds (4240 runs), data profiles tau=1e-3 in groups of n+1; SBJ MDF problem with 11 free variables, 46 EB constraints, 100 random starts, 20,000 budget, profiles tau=5e-2, paired histogram 53/21/26 and a mesh-anisotropy plot (pp. 13-18).
positioning: Continues MADS [6], OrthoMADS [1] and frame-based methods [12]; cites classic scaling texts; the only competitor is its own isotropic version (pp. 6, 12-14).
writing: Contribution sentence plus 'the convergence analysis needs to be entirely revisited'; theory deferred to an appendix; worked 2D example of mesh/frame updates (Fig. 1) (pp. 6, 11-12, 18-20).
limits_future: Priority: adapt the progressive barrier; link anisotropic mesh sizes to variable sensitivities and decomposition methods (pp. 17-18).

method_links.note: Ladder restated and fully re-proved for vector meshes; rational beta^2 defended as necessary by the author's own 2004 counterexample paper.
The performance idea lives in the Poll/mesh geometry, not the Search, at the price of revisiting the whole analysis; Search stays optional.
Budget in n+1 groups, 10 seeds per instance, realistic MDO blackbox with 100 starts and a paired histogram; but same-solver ablation only.
Implemented and released in NOMAD 3.7.x, default by the 3.7.2 guide.
Theory covers EB only, so 46 engineering constraints run under EB with a phase-one start; PB deferred.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: same-solver controlled comparison with shared components
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Quadratic models disabled in both variants and one random-direction generator shared, to isolate the anisotropic mesh
Generalization used to re-present MADS from scratch and drop the unused direction matrix D

transferable: Per-variable scaling from the success direction: after success along d coarsen only coordinates with |d_j| > ||d||_inf/n, with a catch-up rule for lagging coordinates (pp. 11-12).
Initial per-variable step (u_j - l_j)/10, else |x0_j|/10, else 1 (p. 11).
To prove liminf of a vector step size is zero, write components as Delta0_j beta_j^{r_j} with integer r_j and rational beta_j^2 so bounded indices force a finite lattice (pp. 9, 19).
Plot the internal quantity the new mechanism controls (min/max mesh ratio) against evaluations next to the objective (pp. 16-18).
Complement data profiles with a paired per-start histogram of final-value differences and report better/comparable/worse counts (pp. 16-17).

quotes.text: This requirement imposed on the Mads algorithm is not an artifice of the proof since it cannot be relaxed as demonstrated in [4] on an example.
Preliminary tests have shown an influence of the random number generator seed on the data profiles.

title: Optimal adaptive sequential designs for crossover bioequivalence studies
contribution: Optimizes two-stage adaptive bioequivalence designs (methods E and F, with a futility rule and a sample-size cap) over two ISCV ranges by running NOMAD/MADS on a Monte-Carlo/importance-sampling simulator, keeping type I error <= 0.05 and power >= 0.80 while reducing average sample size versus earlier designs B/C/D (read as GERAD G-2015-70).
problem_entry: Sample-size choice under unknown intra-subject CV; earlier designs B, C, D were demonstrations with no optimization and no maximum size (p. 6).
key_idea: Four design variables (alpha1, alpha2, n1, futility f), grid simulation over GMR x ISCV with constraint subsets evaluated first, asymmetric quadratic/linear sample-size cost, and MADS search with infeasible designs given an extremely high cost from a feasible start (pp. 7-12).
assumptions: Normal log-differences with variance 2 sigma^2, Hauschke-based power formula, GMR symmetry, n1 >= 12 (FDA minimum), nmax 42 (cost-equivalent to the smallest SABE study) or 180 (practical); seed handling across variants not stated (pp. 9-11).
proof_devices: importance-sampling estimator with variance no larger than plain Monte Carlo, one run set for both type I error and power (eq. 2, p. 11)
active-constraint argument: optimum lies on the feasibility edge (p. 12)
fold-range argument (5.57x vs 2.95x span of single-stage sizes) explaining n1 over-powering (pp. 15-16)
experiments: About 100 design variants per optimization, ~3 min each, ~5 h on a 5-6 PC cluster; optimized designs hit type I error 0.050 and power 0.80 exactly; sample-size penalty +1.9 (low ISCV) and -6.1/-6.7 (high ISCV) vs single stage, against 4.8-16.3 for B/C/D; no optimizer comparison or restarts (pp. 13-20).
positioning: Extends the same group's Potvin et al. 2008 and Montague et al. 2012 designs; notes Fuglsang's improvements as a different approach; frames ranges around FDA/EMA scaled average BE (pp. 6, 21).
writing: Regulatory-statistics style with flowcharts, tables and a worked example; limits stated concretely; one anomalous table value (0.459) and a MADS citation pointing to the PB paper (pp. 14-22).
limits_future: Power loss when true ISCV exceeds the design range; 'fundamental limitation' of one sequential design over a wide ISCV span; deliberately conservative comparison (pp. 15, 19-20).

method_links.note: A statistical decision procedure's design parameters tuned by MADS with a simulator as blackbox.
Eight quantifiable simulation constraints enforced by an extremely high cost (EB-style) from a feasible start; PB not considered although the optimum lies on the boundary.
Real, expensive, noisy blackbox with an irregular feasibility edge shown and explained.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Type I error and power grid subsets simulated first; remaining grid skipped for infeasible variants

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: asymmetric aggregate over a scenario grid
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Quadratic penalty above the single-stage sample size, linear reward below, averaged over GMR x ISCV so good scenarios cannot buy bad ones

transferable: When each evaluation is a grid of simulations, evaluate constraint-bearing points first and stop at the first violation (p. 10).
For scenario-averaged objectives use an asymmetric per-scenario cost: quadratic above the reference, linear below (eq. 3, p. 12).
Estimate rare-event constraints and power from the same importance-sampled runs, and state where importance sampling fails and what replaces it (p. 11).
Report out-of-range behaviour of the optimized design, not only in-range performance (Table 5, pp. 19-20).
coauthors: J. Xu, C.E. DiLiberti, W.W. Hauck, T.H. Montague, A.F. Parr, D. Potvin, D.J. Schuirmann

quotes.text: Unacceptable designs were assigned an extremely high cost value in order to keep the search within the acceptable region of the design space.
The optimal design will be located on the edge, as otherwise, it can be improved with a larger alpha level or smaller power.
